summary: Intro + quick status; walkthrough of Python + TypeScript integration and auth options; console demo of environment setup and Optimize recommendations; discussion of hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/KMS); agreed next steps for security docs and pilot bench.
topics: Auth options: API keys vs service accounts vs SSO/SAML
Optimize suggestions: batching, KV cache, quantization
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, good to see you. I'm Maya Chen, I'll run through a short integration gardenwalk today. Um, quick round of who is on the line?
[00:12] Carlos: Carlos Rivera, Engineering Manager at GreenBridge.
[00:15] Anya: Anya Petrov, DevOps.
[00:17] Samir: Samir Khan, CTO. Judy from SRE is here too.
[00:22] Maya: Awesome. Quick agenda: 1) show the Python and TypeScript quickstarts, 2) auth & env patterns (how teams put keys in CI), 3) Console and Optimize tips (batching, kv cache), 4) Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:34] Carlos: Sounds good. We're mainly curious about latency tradeoffs and how to run a pilot inside our VPC.
[00:40] Liam: Hey folks, Liam O'Connor here — I'll drive the SDK demo. We'll start with a small Python snippet then switch to a TS example that hooks into your CI.
[00:48] [00:48] Liam: (typing noise) So for Python, you pip install redwood-inference, export REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var; sample code: client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) and then client.generate(...). It's pretty standard.
[01:10] Judy: Do you have a recommended secrets pattern for GitHub Actions? We can't have long-lived keys checked in.
[01:17] Priya: Totally — short lived service accounts are recommended, use the console to mint ephemeral tokens or configure a service principal that rotates. We'll show the console flow in a sec.
[01:27] Liam: For TypeScript it's similar: npm i @redwood/inference, set process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY in your CI secrets, the SDK honors retry/backoff and has streaming support for websockets.
[01:39] Carlos: When you say streaming, is that chunked SSE or websockets? We need to pipe to our UI with low latency.
[01:45] Liam: SSE or websockets both supported — websocket is lower-latency for bi-directional streaming, SSE is simpler for server->client.
[01:52] [02:02] Anya: We're leaning to private deployment because of data residency and KMS control — is that a big lift?
[02:08] Maya: We do private deployments (VPC + on-prem options). Typical lift depends on volume: small POC we can do with a customer-managed control plane and connector to your KMS; larger setups may need dedicated capacity. We'll put together a draft architecture.
[02:24] Samir: Ok, what's the timeline for a pilot? We want to evaluate cost per token and latency SLOs.
[02:30] Maya: Usually 2–4 weeks for a perf pilot: day 1 infra and keys, day 2 run benchmarks, week 1 optimize configs. We'll propose a pilot run in the next message.
[02:41] [03:00] Liam: Jumping back to the SDK: important note — default client settings are safe, but if you're doing high QPS you'll want to tune concurrent streams and the batch size; we also expose KV cache hooks so repeated prompt prefixes can hit cache. Some customers call it K-V cash in notes, so don't worry if you see that in earlier docs.
[03:20] Carlos: KV cache — do you mean prefix caching at serving layer or client-side?
[03:25] Liam: Serving layer. The runtime supports prefix/KV caching — that reduces compute for repeated context. You can also do client side caching for lower tokens but it's less accurate for dynamic contexts.
[03:35] Anya: About quantization — can you run int8 on your dedicated pools? We have older GPUs and want to reduce cost.
[03:42] Priya: Yes, we recommend quantization profiles based on model and sequence length. We can suggest a profile; there are tradeoffs on quality, and our Optimize tool will flag regressions against your eval set.
[03:55] [04:10] Carlos: Can you demo the console flow for creating a service account and configuring a sandbox env?
[04:15] Maya: Yep, switching screens now — (screen sharing) Console > Teams > Service accounts. You can create a service account scoped to particular models and set expiration. For CI you create a token and put it in GH secrets. We also show recommended env variable names and a sample .env.template in the quickstart repo. Link: https://console.redwood.ai/quickstart
[04:45] Judy: For our SSO, we use Okta. How does SAML SSO work for your console?
[04:50] Maya: We support SSO via SAML/Okta, and you can map SCIM groups to RBAC roles in the console so only certain teams can create service accounts or view billing. We'll share the SSO guide.
[05:05] [05:18] Anya: Network egress — if we do private, do you need outbound internet to pull model weights or is everything in a VPC?
[05:24] Priya: With Private deployment you can air-gap model artifact pull or host them in a customer bucket. For hosted we obviously need public endpoints. For VPC we set up private peering and you control KMS.
[05:36] Samir: How are audit logs surfaced? We need request-level logs for compliance.
[05:40] Maya: We have audit trails in the console, plus a log export to your SIEM. You can also configure per-token tracing and we retain them per your retention SLAs.
[05:52] [06:10] Liam: Back to code — quick live example in TypeScript streaming: client.chat.stream(...) and you get incremental tokens; in our Node SDK we expose an on('delta') handler. Some transcriptions call it 'on delta' or 'on data', it's fairly straightforward.
[06:30] Carlos: On cost: how do you show token-level cost? We want to correlate latency with cost.
[06:35] Priya: Console has token-level breakdowns and an estimate per request. Optimize can suggest batching windows and caching to reduce per-token cost; we'll show a sample recommendation card.
[06:50] [07:05] Liam: Example: if you batch 8 requests with similar prompt length you typically reduce the per-token cost by ~30% for our medium models — but there's a latency p99 tradeoff. You can set routing policy to prefer low-latency hosts for critical routes.
[07:25] Carlos: Might need canary/rollback behavior for model upgrades.
[07:29] Maya: We support rollout policies — canary, A/B and automatic fallback to a cheaper model variant under load. We'll include that in the pilot design.
[07:40] [08:10] Anya: For the pilot, we'll want an automated benchmark that measures p50/p95/p99 and token cost, can you provide that?
[08:15] Liam: Yep, that's one of the action items — I'll share a Jupyter + k6 script we use internally. It will include sequence length distributions and batching configs.
[08:30] [09:00] Samir: Security question: KMS — do you support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and customer HSMs?
[09:06] Priya: We integrate with AWS and GCP KMS, and we have HSM integrations for Private deployments. You can also bring your own key material for model encryption.
[09:20] Judy: What about SOC2 scope? We need vendor attestations.
[09:24] Maya: We'll send the SOC2 report and the security questionnaire. That's in the next steps.
[09:33] [10:05] Carlos: Let's walk through a small end-to-end sample: we want to do reranking for search results. How do we set up the SDK and Optimize to recommend batching for short queries?
[10:12] Liam: For reranking with short queries, use embeddings or a lightweight re-ranker model. In the SDK you call client.rerank with an array of candidates; Optimize will analyze token length histogram and recommend small batch windows and prefix caching. We'll show an example in the quickstart repo where batch size is 16 for embeddings and 4 for generation.
[10:40] Anya: Any gotchas with chunked uploads or attachment handling?
[10:44] Liam: Binary payloads go through presigned URLs; for large context use external memory pointers instead of sending the full blob each request. That keeps token count low.
[10:55] [11:20] Maya: Quick pause — any blockers from your side for a pilot?
[11:25] Carlos: We need to confirm legal review timeline and make sure procurement is looped. Also want to see runtime benchmarks first.
[11:32] Maya: Great, we'll attach benchmark results and a proposed SOW.
[11:38] [12:00] Priya: On instrumentation — we can drop tracing hooks in the SDK and emit to your trace collector, but we also have built-in traces in the console with token-level timelines.
[12:15] Samir: For deterministic evals, how do you handle eval drift when you change quantization?
[12:20] Liam: Optimize ties regressions to your prompt sets and alerts on quality drops; it can auto-snapshot against a baseline and flag if quantized models drop below thresholds.
[12:34] [13:00] Anya: Ok, about cost controls — can we cap spend per service account?
[13:04] Maya: Yes, per-token quotas and rate limits per token can be set on service accounts. We can also set route-level throttles for critical endpoints.
[13:15] Carlos: If we start hosted then move to private, how painful is migration of models and configs?
[13:20] Priya: We've designed deployment abstraction so you can pin model versions and configs — migration is mostly infra (VPC, KMS) plus swapping endpoints. We have migration docs and a migration runbook we'll share.
[13:34] [14:00] Liam: Live snippet for CI: in GitHub Actions you set REDWOOD_API_KEY as a secret, reference it in action and the SDK will respect NODE_ENV for streaming toggles. Example action: uses: actions/setup-node; env: REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY }}; run: node scripts/run-bench.js
[14:25] Judy: Does the SDK include client-side retry logic for 429s?
[14:29] Liam: Yes it has exponential backoff with jitter and you can override thresholds. For hard rate limits we suggest using client-side queuing plus server-side batching.
[14:42] [15:10] Carlos: For the pilot we'll want an architecture diagram. Who builds that?
[15:14] Maya: We'll draft one — I'll include a recommended topology for VPC peering, KMS, and service account roles.
[15:22] Anya: Also need firewall rules and Egress IPs.
[15:26] Priya: We'll list expected CIDR ranges and egress IPs in the doc.
[15:33] [16:00] (brief side conversation, crosstalk)
[16:22] Samir: One more: latency targets — we need p95 under 220 ms for 512-token prompts, is that achievable?
[16:30] Liam: For hosted low-latency pools yes, often p95 in 150–200ms for medium models at that token length; dedicated capacity can be tuned further. We'll validate in the benchmark.
[16:45] [17:00] Maya: Ok wrapping up — to recap next steps: Maya to send security pack and quickstart links; Liam to send benchmark scripts and example console screenshots; Anya to provide VPC/KMS details; schedule pilot kickoff (tentative week of 12/08).
[17:18] Carlos: Thanks all, that was helpful.
[17:22] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite and the doc bundle.
[17:28] (meeting ends)
questions: What is the recommended pattern for CI secrets and short-lived tokens?
Can Redwood run quantized models on our older GPUs?
How are audit logs exported to our SIEM?
